WORK BRIEF
Tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling bewilderment that turns to sharp absurdity at court.
Depiction rules:
- Alice's changing size reads clearly against doors, furniture, trees and other figures.
- Talking animals are drawn as animals, with human posture and dress where the text gives it.
- Playing-card courtiers, gardeners and soldiers are flat, oblong cards with heads, arms and legs.
- Threats and executions stay threats or slapstick; no gore or real injury.
- Take no likeness, costume or prop from film or animated adaptations.
Era: Victorian England and its dream Wonderland. People: Alice, a young Victorian English girl, among talking animals, card courtiers and odd Wonderland folk. Dress: A Victorian child's dress and pinafore for Alice; period robes, waistcoats and hats for others. Technology: Pocket watches, oil lamps, slates and pencils; no machines or modern devices.
STORY SECTION: Alice and the Cheshire Cat

MOMENT (The Queen’s Croquet-Ground ¶49 to The Queen’s Croquet-Ground ¶51): “How do you like the Queen?” said the Cat in a low voice. “Not at all,” said Alice: “she’s so extremely—” Just then she noticed that the Queen was close behind her, listening: so she went on, “—likely to win, that it’s hardly worth while finishing the game.” The Queen smiled and passed on.
PREVIOUS: “I don’t think they play at all fairly,” Alice began, in rather a complaining tone, “and they all quarrel so dreadfully one can’t hear oneself speak—and they don’t seem to have any rules in particular; at least, if there are, nobody attends to them—and you’ve no idea how confusing it is all the things being alive; for instance, there’s the arch I’ve got to go through next walking about at the othe
NEXT: “Who _are_ you talking to?” said the King, going up to Alice, and looking at the Cat’s head with great curiosity.

STORY SECTION: Talk with the Cheshire Cat

MOMENT (Pig and Pepper ¶50 to Pig and Pepper ¶52): The Cat only grinned when it saw Alice. It looked good-natured, she thought: still it had _very_ long claws and a great many teeth, so she felt that it ought to be treated with respect. “Cheshire Puss,” she began, rather timidly, as she did not at all know whether it would like the name: however, it only grinned a little wider. “Come, it’s pleased so far,” thought Alice, and she went on. “Would you tell me, please, which way I ought to go from here?” “That depends a good deal on where you want to get to,” said the Cat.
PREVIOUS: (section starts here)
NEXT: “I don’t much care where—” said Alice.

STORY SECTION: The Dormouse's treacle-well story

MOMENT (A Mad Tea-Party ¶70 to A Mad Tea-Party ¶81): “Once upon a time there were three little sisters,” the Dormouse began in a great hurry; “and their names were Elsie, Lacie, and Tillie; and they lived at the bottom of a well—” “What did they live on?” said Alice, who always took a great interest in questions of eating and drinking. “They lived on treacle,” said the Dormouse, after thinking a minute or two. “They couldn’t have done that, you know,” Alice gently remarked; “they’d have been ill.” “So they were,” said the Dormouse; “_very_ ill.” Alice tried to fancy to herself what such an extraordinary way of living would be like, but it puzzled her too much, so she went on: “But why did they live at the bottom of a well?” “Take some more tea,” the March Hare said to Alice, very earnestly. “I’ve had nothing yet,” Alice replied in an offended tone, “so I can’t take more.” “You mean you can’t take _less_,” said the Hatter: “it’s very easy to take _more_ than nothing.” “Nobody asked _your_ opinion,” said Alice. “Who’s making personal remarks now?” the Hatter asked triumphantly. Alice did not quite know what to say to this: so she helped herself to some tea and bread-and-butter, and then turned to the Dormouse, and repeated her question. “Why did they live at the bottom of a well?”
PREVIOUS: “And be quick about it,” added the Hatter, “or you’ll be asleep again before it’s done.”
NEXT: The Dormouse again took a minute or two to think about it, and then said, “It was a treacle-well.”

Tone: Reverent, grounded and epic; grief, hope and human dignity without spectacle.
Depiction rules:
- God the Father has no human face or body; use light, cloud, fire or radiance. The Holy Spirit is dove, wind or flame, never human.
- Treat battles, death and crucifixion seriously; avoid lingering gore.
- No sexually explicit content; non-sexual nudity may follow the text.
- Show all peoples with dignity, without ethnic or religious caricature.
- Visionary creatures follow the text, strange and fearsome rather than comic.
Era: Egypt, wilderness and settlement. People: Israelites, Egyptians and neighboring ancient peoples. Dress: Woven tunics, cloaks, Egyptian linen and priestly garments. Technology: Bronze tools, chariots and early iron; no modern objects.
STORY SECTION: Guidance by the cloud and fire

MOMENT (Numbers 9:22): Whether it was two days, or a month, or a year that the cloud stayed on the tabernacle, remaining on it, the children of Israel remained encamped, and didn’t travel; but when it was taken up, they traveled.
PREVIOUS: Sometimes the cloud was from evening until morning; and when the cloud was taken up in the morning, they traveled; or by day and by night, when the cloud was taken up, they traveled.
NEXT: At the commandment of Yahweh they encamped, and at the commandment of Yahweh they traveled. They kept Yahweh’s command, at the commandment of Yahweh by Moses.
